forbidden_claims.statement_nl: Let $n$ be an integer greater than 1. For which real numbers $x$ is \\[\\lfloor nx \\rfloor - \\sum_{k=1}^{n} \\frac{\\lfloor kx \\rfloor}{k}\\] maximal, and what is the maximal value that this expression can take?

payload.previous_feedback: Previous vetter reason: The argument is correct: for r in [0,1), setting m=floor(nr) gives m/n<=r, hence k(m/n)<=kr for each 1<=k<=n, so floor(km/n)<=floor(kr). Since floor(n(m/n))=m=floor(nr), termwise comparison yields f_n(r)<=f_n(m/n). This matches the stated lemma exactly, with no dependency issues.
payload.previous_proof_nl:
Fix an integer n > 1, and define f_n(x) = floor(nx) - sum_{k=1}^n floor(kx)/k. Let r be any real number with 0 <= r < 1, and set m = floor(nr). We must show f_n(r) <= f_n(m/n).

Since m = floor(nr), we have m <= nr < m+1. Dividing by n > 0 gives m/n <= r. Therefore, for each integer k with 1 <= k <= n, multiplying by k preserves the inequality:
k(m/n) <= kr.
Because the floor function is monotone nondecreasing on R, it follows that
floor(k(m/n)) <= floor(kr)
for every k = 1, ..., n.

Also, m is an integer, so
floor(n(m/n)) = floor(m) = m = floor(nr).

Now compare the two values:
f_n(r) = floor(nr) - sum_{k=1}^n floor(kr)/k
<= m - sum_{k=1}^n floor(k(m/n))/k
= floor(n(m/n)) - sum_{k=1}^n floor(k(m/n))/k
= f_n(m/n).

This is exactly the desired inequality.

result_payload.proof_nl:
Fix an integer n > 1 and define f_n(x) = floor(nx) - sum_{k=1}^n floor(kx)/k. Let r be any real number with 0 <= r < 1, and set m = floor(nr). We will show that f_n(r) <= f_n(m/n).

Since m = floor(nr), we have m <= nr < m+1. Dividing by n > 0 gives m/n <= r. Now fix any k in {1,2,...,n}. Multiplying by the positive number k preserves the inequality, so k(m/n) <= kr. Because the floor function is nondecreasing on the real numbers, it follows that floor(k(m/n)) <= floor(kr) for every such k.

Also, m is an integer, so floor(n(m/n)) = floor(m) = m = floor(nr).

Therefore, term by term,
sum_{k=1}^n floor(k(m/n))/k <= sum_{k=1}^n floor(kr)/k.
Using the equality of the first terms, we obtain
f_n(r) = floor(nr) - sum_{k=1}^n floor(kr)/k = m - sum_{k=1}^n floor(kr)/k
<= m - sum_{k=1}^n floor(k(m/n))/k
= floor(n(m/n)) - sum_{k=1}^n floor(k(m/n))/k
= f_n(m/n).

This is exactly the claimed inequality.
